key_takeaways: Library visitation peaked in the early 2010s (~53% of adults, ~3.85 per-capita IMLS visits in FY2019) and declined sharply during COVID-19 (2.01 per-capita in FY2022), with partial recovery by FY2024 (2.53 per-capita).
In 2022, the NEA SPPA (a Census Bureau CPS supplement) found 23% of adults visited a public library in the prior 12 months - the first time this question was asked.
Gallup (2019) found visiting the library was the most common cultural activity, averaging 10.5 visits/adult/year - more than double movie theater visits (5.3).
Women visit libraries nearly twice as often as men (Gallup: 13.4 vs 7.5; Pew: 57% vs lower for men). Low-income households visit most frequently.
Book reading has declined: 48.5% of adults read any book in 2022 (down from 54.6% in 2012). Novel/short-story reading hit a record low of 37.6%.
Print books remain dominant (64% read print in 2025 vs 31% e-book, 26% audiobook), but digital formats have grown substantially since 2011.
The main reasons for library visits are borrowing printed books (64% of visitors), reading/studying (49%), and getting help from librarians (35%).
Libraries are highly valued: 95-94% say libraries improve community quality of life; 66% say closing would majorly impact their community.
There are approximately 133,200 librarians/media collections specialists and ~402,590 core library workers (BLS OES 2024). IMLS reports 143,324 total public library staff (FY2024).

Library computer/internet access serves a critical equity role: ~23% of all Americans 16+ used library computers/internet/Wi-Fi (Pew 2016); 77 million used library computers/wireless (Gates Foundation 2010).

historical_growth.event: Library of Congress founded (April 24, 1800) with an appropriation of $5,000; initial collection of 740 books and 3 maps.
British troops burned the Capitol, destroying the Library's core collection of 3,000 volumes (August 24, 1814).
Congress approved purchase of Thomas Jefferson's personal library of 6,487 books for $23,950 (January 30, 1815).
Library moved into its own building (now the Thomas Jefferson Building), completed 1890-1897.
John Adams Building opened to the public (January 3, 1939).
James H. Billington became 13th Librarian of Congress; analog collections stood at 85.5 million items.
Analog collections exceeded 160 million items, having doubled under Billington (1987-2015).
Carla Hayden became 14th Librarian of Congress (first woman and first African American in the role).

narrative_facts: Approximately half of the Library's book and serial collections are in languages other than English; collections contain materials in some 470 languages.
The Law Library of Congress is the world's largest law library.
The Library holds the largest rare-book collection in North America, including the largest collection of 15th-century books in the Western Hemisphere.
The Geography and Map Division holds the world's largest collection of cartographic materials.
The Prints and Photographs Division contains millions of visual images.
Each working day the Library receives some 15,000 items and adds roughly 10,000 to its collections (per fascinating-facts page).

nlm.description: The National Library of Medicine (NLM), operated by the United States federal government, is the world's largest biomedical library. Located on the campus of the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, NLM has been a center of information innovation since its founding in 1836. It maintains and makes available a vast print collection and produces electronic information services on a wide range of topics that are searched billions of times each year by millions of people around the globe. NLM also supports and conducts research, development, and training in biomedical informatics and health information technology, and coordinates an 8,000+ member Network of the National Library of Medicine that promotes and provides access to health information in communities across the United States.

key_databases.name: PubMed
key_databases.description: A free database primarily including the MEDLINE database of references and abstracts on life sciences and biomedical topics. Maintained by NLM at NIH as part of the Entrez system of information retrieval. First released January 1996; offered free to the public starting June 1997.
key_databases.size: More than 40 million citations and abstracts (as of March 2025)
key_databases.size_detail: 40M+ citations dating back to 1966, selectively to 1865, and highly selectively to 1809. 24.6 million records with abstracts (2023). 26.8 million records with links to full-text versions, of which 10.9 million available full-text for free (2023).

key_databases.name: MEDLINE
key_databases.description: Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online. A bibliographic database of life sciences and biomedical information covering medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, veterinary medicine, and health care. The online version of MEDLARS, launched in 1971; compiled by NLM and freely searchable via PubMed.
key_databases.size_detail: 29M+ references covering 1946-present. Updated daily with 2,000-4,000 references per update. Covers 40 languages for current journals, 60 for older journals. Over 93% of records are published in English.
key_databases.history: MEDLARS launched 1964 as first large-scale computer-based retrospective search service; online version (MEDLINE) began late 1971

key_databases.name: PubMed Central (PMC)
key_databases.description: A free digital repository that archives openly accessible full-text scholarly articles published in biomedical and life sciences journals. More than a document repository - submissions are indexed and formatted for enhanced metadata, medical ontology, and unique identifiers. A major research database developed by NCBI.
key_databases.history: Began as E-biomed, proposed May 1999 by then-NIH director Harold Varmus. Hosts access to human genome (2000). 2008 NIH Public Access Policy mandated NIH-funded research be available on PMC within 12 months of publication.

key_databases.name: ClinicalTrials.gov
key_databases.description: A registry of clinical trials run by NLM at NIH. Launched February 29, 2000 following the Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997. Expanded by FDA Amendments Act of 2007 to require registration and results reporting.

key_databases.name: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)
key_databases.description: An intramural division within NLM that creates public databases in molecular biology, conducts research in computational biology, develops software tools for analyzing molecular and genomic data, and disseminates biomedical information. Founded November 4, 1988 through legislation sponsored by Congressman Claude Pepper.
key_databases.size: Houses multiple major databases including GenBank, PubMed, PMC, and dozens of others

key_databases.name: GenBank
key_databases.description: An open access, annotated collection of publicly available nucleotide sequences and their protein translations. Part of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC). Produced and maintained by NCBI at NLM/NIH. Established in 1982 by Walter Goad at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
key_databases.size: 53.90 trillion bases in 6.27 billion sequence records (release 271, April 2026)
key_databases.size_detail: Traditional GenBank entries: 261,460,182 records containing 7,289,942,983,522 base pairs (April 2026). Combined with WGS: 45,628,511,953,497 bases in 4,756,526,485 sequences. Includes sequences from more than 581,000 formally described species. Doubles approximately every 18 months.

key_databases.name: MedlinePlus
key_databases.description: An online consumer health information service produced by NLM. Provides curated consumer health information in English and Spanish with select content in additional languages. Brings together information from NLM, NIH, other U.S. government agencies, and health-related organizations. Introduced October 1998.
key_databases.size: Almost 1,000 health topics in English and Spanish, with links to health information in over 40 languages

key_databases.name: MeSH (Medical Subject Headings)
key_databases.description: The NLM controlled vocabulary thesaurus used for indexing articles for PubMed/MEDLINE. A comprehensive life science vocabulary that enables consistent retrieval of biomedical literature.

key_databases.name: ChemIDplus
key_databases.description: A chemical database of over 400,000 chemicals complete with names, synonyms, and structures. Includes links to NLM and other databases and resources, including federal, state, and international agencies.

key_databases.name: LocatorPlus
key_databases.description: NLM's online catalog, providing access to the library's collection holdings.

key_databases.name: TOXNET (Toxicology Data Network)
key_databases.description: Toxicology and environmental health information system established at NLM in 1967. Includes databases compiled from medical literature and governmental/nongovernmental organization files for chemical emergency response and public education.

historical_timeline.event: Founded as the Library of the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army with $150 for medical books; first catalog of books issued in 1840
Library moved to Riggs Bank Building at 15th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, NW, Washington, DC
Lieutenant John Shaw Billings appointed to take charge of the collection, marking a turning point in the library's development
Library moved to Ford's Theatre (after Lincoln's assassination) at 513 10th Street NW, Washington, DC; remained until 1887
Billings began Index Medicus, the first comprehensive index of journal articles; predecessor to MEDLINE
Index-Catalogue launched, a combined author and subject catalog of the library's growing collection
Library moved to Army Medical Museum and Library Building at 7th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC (remained until 1962)
By Billings' departure, holdings reached 116,847 books and 191,598 pamphlets; transformed into the world's greatest medical library
Officially renamed the Army Medical Library
Library transferred from Department of Defense to the Public Health Service and renamed the National Library of Medicine via Public Law 941 (August 3, 1956)
Library took first steps into the computer age, launching a mechanized system for producing its publications
Library moved to its current quarters on the NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland
MEDLARS (Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System) launched as the first large-scale, computer-based retrospective search service available to the general public; cost $3 million to develop
Toxicology and Environmental Health Program established at NLM
MEDLINE (MEDLARS Online) became available for online searching from remote medical libraries; initially covered 239 journals
Director Donald Lindberg's Grateful Med project facilitated direct, affordable access to the MEDLINE database
National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) established within NLM (November 4, 1988) through legislation by Congressman Claude Pepper
NCBI team developed the BLAST tool for comparing biological sequences
NCBI established a website for online access to BLAST, GenBank, and the Entrez retrieval system
PubMed first released in January 1996, ushering in free home and office-based MEDLINE searching
PubMed offered free to the public starting June 1997
MedlinePlus introduced in October 1998 to provide consumer-friendly health information
PubMed Central launched; ClinicalTrials.gov made available to the public on February 29, 2000; NCBI hosted access to the human genome
Last printed issue of Index Medicus published in December 2004, replaced by freely accessible PubMed

trend_summary.note: Earliest PLS vintage in this dataset; modest ILL volume.
Rapid growth phase: borrowed rose from 16.3M to 55.5M (+241%) as OCLC resource sharing became ubiquitous and ILLiad workflows matured.
Plateau/peak era; total ILL transactions peaked at ~141.5M in FY2013 (borrowed 70.7M, lent 70.8M).
Flat at ~140M total; first signs of softening as e-book and digital-licensing access began substituting for some returnable ILL.
Notable step-down to 128.5M (from 140.8M in 2016, -8.7%), the first sharp decline -- coincides with maturation of statewide e-book platforms and ebook lending.
COVID-19 disruption: fell to 99.7M total (-29.5% from FY2013 peak; -27.3% vs FY2019) as buildings closed and physical shipping halted.
Recovery: rebounded to 130.1M (2021), dipped to 118.3M (2022), 123.1M (2023), and 137.3M (2024) -- essentially back to pre-pandemic levels but still below the 2013 peak.
FY2024 borrowed (70.74M) exceeded FY2013's borrowed total, making FY2024 the highest borrowed-year on record; lent (66.6M) remained below the 2013 lent peak.
Over 24 years borrowed grew +335% and lent +305%, but most growth occurred 2000-2013; the 2017-2022 era shows structural softening partly offset by 2024 recovery.

by_state.source: IMLS Public Libraries Survey FY2024, LOANFM and LOANTO aggregated by state (STABR)
by_state.note: State rankings reflect both library-system density and how aggressively a state routes intra-state requests through ILL rather than consortial shared catalogs. Ohio, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, New York and Illinois dominate because of mature statewide resource-sharing backbones (e.g., OhioLINK, WiLS, MassBLRC/MLS, NYPL/NY3Rs, ILDS/ILLINET). Territories (AS, GU, MP, PR, VI) and HI/DC report near-zero ILL through PLS.

networks.name: OCLC Resource Sharing Network
networks.description: World's largest ILL network; the backbone of U.S. and global interlibrary loan. Lenders/borrowers are matched through the WorldCat union catalog. Successor products Tipasa and WorldShare ILL replaced the legacy OCLC ILL messaging service.

networks.name: RapidILL
networks.description: Unmediated, automated ILL/document-delivery system developed at Colorado State University in 1997 after the Spring Creek flood destroyed journal holdings. Known for very fast turnaround and high automation. Acquired by Ex Libris in 2019 and now offered alongside Rapido.

networks.name: Libraries Very Interested in Sharing (LVIS)
networks.description: An OCLC resource-sharing 'group' whose members agree to lend to one another for free (no per-transaction fee), reducing ILL costs among participants.

networks.name: OCLC Express
networks.description: An OCLC program for libraries that commit to 18-hour-or-less turnaround; Express libraries receive priority routing of copy requests.

networks.name: Center for Research Libraries (CRL)
networks.description: A global consortium of university, college and research libraries (75+ years) that operates a buy-in shared-collection model; members borrow from CRL's deep holdings of newspapers, foreign dissertations, archival microforms, and rare materials not held elsewhere.

networks.name: Research Libraries Group (RLG)
networks.description: Former major academic-library resource-sharing network (RLG ILL) and union catalog (RLIN). Merged into OCLC in July 2006; its user base was folded into the OCLC resource-sharing network.

networks.name: Maine InfoNet
networks.description: Maine's statewide library network. Operates MaineCat (a statewide union catalog combining 100+ library collections in 10 large online systems), Minerva (a shared ILS for 60+ libraries of all types), URSUS/MILS (shared catalogs), and the Download Library / Digital Maine Library (shared e-book/e-audio collection).

networks.name: National Network of Libraries of Medicine (NNLM) / DOCLINE
networks.description: The U.S. medical-library resource-sharing network coordinated by the National Library of Medicine. NLM developed DOCLINE, a specialized request-routing system for biomedical document delivery among NNLM member libraries.

networks.name: Amigos Library Services
networks.description: Regional library cooperative (successor to AMIGOS Bibliographic Council) providing OCLC billing/cataloging support and resource-sharing services to member libraries, primarily in the Southwest.

networks.name: State-level consortia / backbones
networks.description: Many of the highest-ILL states owe their volume to statewide consortial backbones: OhioLINK (OH), WiLS (WI), Massachusetts Library System (MA), Empire State Library Network/NY3Rs (NY), ILDS/ILLINET (IL), PALCI (PA), MCLS (MI), CARLI (IL academic), etc. These route intra-state requests cheaply, inflating PLS ILL counts relative to states that rely on direct OCLC requests.

academic_libraries_arl.source: Association of Research Libraries (ARL) Statistics, published annually since 1963 (ARL assumed responsibility for annual library statistics that year).
academic_libraries_arl.latest_publication: ARL Statistics 2024 (published 2025), describing collections, staffing, expenditures and service activities of 124 ARL member libraries in the U.S. (plus Canadian members reported separately).
academic_libraries_arl.metrics_tracked: ARL Statistics include interlibrary loan (borrowed and lent) and document delivery as distinct service metrics for research libraries -- the returnable (book) vs non-returnable (document/article) split is captured here rather than in IMLS PLS.
academic_libraries_arl.access_note: ARL Statistics tables are a member/paywalled publication; transaction-level totals are not freely available online. IMLS PLS (this file) covers public libraries only, so academic ILL volume is NOT included in the national_totals above.

document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.summary: IMLS PLS does NOT split returnable (physical book) from non-returnable (document/article) ILL; both are counted together in LOANFM/LOANTO. The split is tracked by OCLC (Tipasa/WorldShare ILL) and ARL Statistics.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.oclc_e_resource_requests_per_year: 3,000,000+ (OCLC WorldShare ILL) -- a proxy for non-returnable / document-delivery volume through OCLC.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.oclc_physical_loans_estimate: The bulk of the ~140M annual PLS transactions are returnable physical loans (books/media shipped between public libraries), since public-library ILL is dominated by print monographs; OCLC's 3M+ e-resource figure is a small fraction of total public-library ILL.
document_delivery_vs_book_breakdown.trend_note: Over time the share of non-returnable (article/document delivery) has fallen as more journal content is licensed directly via database subscriptions; conversely, e-book and digital-audio circulation (316M ebook + 245M e-audio circulations in FY2024 per IMLS PLS digital file) now substitutes for some returnable book ILL -- one structural reason ILL plateaued 2014-2017.

digital_resource_context_fy2024.source: IMLS PLS FY2024 electronic-services data (this project's data/pls_fy2024_digital.json)
digital_resource_context_fy2024.interpretation: Public libraries circulated ~555M electronic items in FY2024 -- roughly 4x the total national ILL volume (137M). The expansion of direct e-licensing and statewide shared e-book platforms is the main structural pressure reducing growth in returnable book ILL, even as overall ILL has recovered post-COVID.

key_facts: U.S. public libraries reported 137,344,470 interlibrary-loan transactions in FY2024 (70.74M borrowed, 66.60M lent) -- IMLS Public Libraries Survey.
ILL peaked at ~141.5M total transactions in FY2013, dipped during COVID to 99.7M in FY2020 (-29.5% from peak), and recovered to 137.3M by FY2024.
FY2024 set the record for 'borrowed' (materials received via ILL) at 70.74M, surpassing FY2013; 'lent' (66.6M) remained below the 2013 peak of 70.8M.

Over 24 years (FY2000->FY2024) total public-library ILL grew +318% (borrowed +335%, lent +305%), but nearly all growth occurred 2000-2013; the post-2013 era shows plateau/decline partly offset by post-COVID recovery.

OCLC operates the world's largest resource-sharing network: 10,000+ libraries in 50+ countries, delivering 3M+ e-resource ILL requests per year; OCLC itself has ~30,000 member libraries in 100+ countries.
OCLC's Express program (1,000+ libraries) fills copy requests in an average of 10 hours; some e-resource requests deliver in 15 minutes.
LVIS (Libraries Very Interested in Sharing), an OCLC free-lending group, has 2,200 participating libraries.
RapidILL, an automated unmediated ILL system developed at Colorado State University in 1997, has 300+ member libraries and was acquired by Ex Libris in 2019.
The ALA Interlibrary Loan Code for the United States (maintained by RUSA STARS, first national code 1917, current revision 2016) governs U.S. ILL practice.
Research Libraries Group (RLG) merged into OCLC in July 2006, consolidating U.S. academic-library resource sharing onto the OCLC network.
Ohio is the #1 ILL state by volume (FY2024: 8.76M borrowed, 8.75M lent) thanks to the OhioLINK consortium backbone; Wisconsin, Massachusetts, New York and Illinois round out the top 5.

Academic-library ILL is tracked separately by the ARL Statistics (124 U.S. ARL member libraries, latest edition ARL Statistics 2024) and captures the returnable-vs-document-delivery split that IMLS PLS does not.

IMLS PLS does NOT separate returnable (physical book) from non-returnable (document/article) ILL; both are counted in the LOANFM/LOANTO totals. OCLC reports 3M+ e-resource (largely non-returnable) requests/year as a partial proxy.
Public libraries circulated ~555M electronic items (ebooks, e-audio, e-video) in FY2024 -- about 4x the national ILL volume -- illustrating how direct e-licensing now substitutes for some ILL demand.
The borrowed/lent ratio has stayed near 1.0 for two decades (FY2024: 1.06), reflecting that ILL is a reciprocal exchange: libraries borrow roughly as much as they lend.
methodology_and_caveats: national_totals and by_state are computed directly from IMLS Public Libraries Survey microdata (FY2000-FY2024), fields LOANFM and LOANTO, in this project's data/pls_trends_national.csv and data/pls_trends_by_state.csv (generated by scripts/parse_pls_historical.py).

PLS covers U.S. public library administrative entities only (9,249 systems in FY2024). Academic, special, school, and medical libraries are excluded -- so the national total UNDERCOUNTS total U.S. ILL activity.
PLS uses negative sentinels (-1/-3/-9) for missing data; these are treated as zero/missing in aggregation, so a few non-reporting systems contribute 0 (a slight undercount).
OCLC figures are self-reported by OCLC on its product/about pages and the OCLC Wikipedia article (citing OCLC's 2020-21 annual report); they describe the global network, not U.S.-only volume.
ARL Statistics (academic research libraries) is a paywalled publication; exact academic ILL transaction counts were not freely retrievable online and are therefore referenced qualitatively.
The returnable vs non-returnable (document delivery) split is not available in PLS; the breakdown here is inferred from OCLC's 3M+ e-resource figure and industry knowledge, not a direct PLS count.

prison_libraries.topic: Prison libraries and library services to incarcerated people in the United States
prison_libraries.data_availability: There is NO single comprehensive national dataset on prison libraries. The Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) collects prison and prisoner counts but does NOT systematically collect library-access data. The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) operates libraries in federal facilities but publishes no public inventory of them. State departments of corrections vary widely and most do not report library statistics. The figures below are compiled from BJS prison-population reports, ALA reports and standards, NIC topic resources, congressional press releases and bill text, Ithaka S+R research, and journalism. Where a number is an estimate or derived figure, it is flagged as such.

prison_counts.facility_census_note: The Census of State and Federal Adult Correctional Facilities is collected periodically (last published for 2019). BJS confirms it covers facility counts, programs, staff, and resources, but the 2019 detailed tables were not directly retrievable via the targeted URLs during this research. The widely cited figure from the 2019 census is approximately 1,677 state and federal correctional facilities. State prisons are operated by 50 state departments of corrections plus the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP).
prison_counts.data_source: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Prisons Report Series: Preliminary Data Release, 2023 (NCJ 309396)

library_access.official_access_rate_note: No federal statistical agency publishes the percentage of U.S. prisons with library services. BJS collects prison and prisoner counts but not library-access data; BOP does not publish a public inventory of facility libraries; state departments of corrections report inconsistently. The figures below are qualitative findings and informal estimates, not official statistics.
library_access.ala_finding_on_service_quality: ALA (2025) reports that many so-called prison libraries are 'little more than a few dusty shelves, often not managed by trained library workers.' Some prisons have libraries 'worthy of the name,' but many others have 'only minimal or nonexistent services,' meaning many incarcerated people have 'no real access to a meaningful library and the expertise of librarians.'
library_access.ithaka_finding_on_law_vs_recreational: Ithaka S+R (2024) found that in some facilities the law library is effectively the only library resource, because departments of corrections are generally obligated to provide legal-access resources, while recreational reading libraries are 'effectively non-existent.'
library_access.filter_estimate_basis: Using ALA's $13/capita adequate-funding benchmark against the $60M over six years, the Act might fund services at roughly 500 facilities - about one-third of state prisons. This is an informal journalist estimate, not an official projection.
library_access.prison_library_staffing_range: Ithaka S+R (2024): staffing ranges from a professional librarian to a correctional officer to incarcerated individuals themselves. Many prison libraries depend on donations and outside organizations (including public libraries) for books and resources.
library_access.training_gap: Ithaka S+R (2024): none of the interviewed librarians had received specific training in prison librarianship; it is usually treated as a 'special library' topic in library schools with few training opportunities.
library_access.covid_impact: Ithaka S+R (2024): during COVID-19 many prison libraries were closed completely or sectioned off for social distancing, and prison libraries were impacted the most when departments of corrections made budget and staffing cuts.

state_level_data.note: No comparable state-level dataset on prison library access exists. Each state department of corrections sets its own policies on library hours, budgets, staffing, and technology, and most do not report library statistics. BJS publishes state-level prisoner counts but not library-access figures. The examples below are documented programs found in the research, not a complete inventory.
